"'''Crazy Little Thing Called Love'''" is a song by the British [[rock music|rock]] band [[Queen (band)|Queen]]. Written by [[Freddie Mercury]] in 1979, the track appears on their 1980 album ''[[The Game (Queen album)|The Game]]''. It reached number two in the [[UK singles chart]] in late 1979, before becoming the group's first number-one single on the [[Billboard Hot 100|US ''Billboard'' Hot 100]] in early 1980, where it remained for four consecutive weeks.<ref name="Billboard">[[Joel Whitburn|Whitburn, Joel]] (2006). The ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' Book of Top 40 Hits. Billboard Books</ref><ref name="UKSingles">Roberts, David (2006). [[British Hit Singles & Albums]]. London: Guinness World Records Limited</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Anderson |first=Trevor |date=February 23, 2018 |title=Rewinding the Charts: In 1980, Queen Got ‘Crazy’ Atop the Hot 100 |url=https://www.billboard.com/pro/queen-crazy-little-thing-called-love-hot-100-number-1-rewinding-charts/ |access-date= |website=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]] |language=en-US}}</ref> The song was Queen's final single release of the [[1970s in music|1970s]] and was later included on their 1981 compilation album ''[[Greatest Hits (Queen album)|Greatest Hits]]''. 

Having composed "Crazy Little Thing Called Love" on guitar, Mercury played rhythm guitar while performing the song live between 1979 and 1986, marking the second instrument he played onstage with Queen besides the piano.<ref name="Circus">[http://www.queenonline.com/en/the-band/interviews/queen/circus-1980/ Lights! Action! Sound! It's That Crazy Little Thing Called Queen] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110628080136/http://www.queenonline.com/en/the-band/interviews/queen/circus-1980/ |date=28 June 2011 }} Circus Magazine. Retrieved 29 June 2011</ref> Official live recordings of the song appear on ''[[Queen Rock Montreal]]'', ''[[Queen on Fire – Live at the Bowl]]'', [[Live Aid#Official Live Aid DVD|''Live Aid'']], ''[[Live at Wembley '86]]'', and ''[[Hungarian Rhapsody: Queen Live in Budapest]]''.<ref>{{cite web|author=Stephen Thomas Erlewine |url=http://www.allmusic.com/album/r1239496 |title=Queen Rock Montreal – Queen | Songs, Reviews, Credits |website=[[AllMusic]] |date=30 October 2007 |access-date=14 October 2016|author-link=Stephen Thomas Erlewine }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ultimatequeen.co.uk/songs/wembley.htm#under |title=Queen "Live At Wembley 1986 / Live At Wembley Stadium" album and song lyrics |website=Ultimatequeen.co.uk |access-date=14 October 2016}}</ref> The song was also performed at [[The Freddie Mercury Tribute Concert]] on 20 April 1992, with [[Robert Plant]] joining Queen on vocals.<ref name="Tribute">{{cite web|url=http://www.ultimatequeen.co.uk/videos/fmtributedvd.htm#crazy |title=Queen "The Freddie Mercury Tribute Concert" video and song lyrics |website=Ultimatequeen.co.uk |access-date=14 October 2016}}</ref> Since then, it has been covered by a number of artists, including [[Dwight Yoakam]], [[Michael Bublé]], [[Diana Ross]], [[Maroon 5]], and [[Brett Eldredge]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Covers of Crazy Little Thing Called Love by Queen |url=https://www.whosampled.com/Queen/Crazy-Little-Thing-Called-Love/covered/ |access-date= |website=WhoSampled |language=en}}</ref>

"Crazy Little Thing Called Love" is a song by the British rock band Queen. Written by Freddie Mercury in 1979, the track appears on their 1980 album The Game. It reached number two in the UK singles chart in late 1979, before becoming the group's first number-one single on the US Billboard Hot 100 in early 1980, where it remained for four consecutive weeks. The song was Queen's final single release of the 1970s and was later included on their 1981 compilation album Greatest Hits. 

Having composed "Crazy Little Thing Called Love" on guitar, Mercury played rhythm guitar while performing the song live between 1979 and 1986, marking the second instrument he played onstage with Queen besides the piano. Official live recordings of the song appear on Queen Rock Montreal, Queen on Fire – Live at the Bowl, Live Aid, Live at Wembley '86, and Hungarian Rhapsody: Queen Live in Budapest. The song was also performed at The Freddie Mercury Tribute Concert on 20 April 1992, with Robert Plant joining Queen on vocals. Since then, it has been covered by a number of artists, including Dwight Yoakam, Michael Bublé, Diana Ross, Maroon 5, and Brett Eldredge.

sections.heading: Composition
sections.wikitext:
The song was written by Mercury as a tribute to his musical heroes [[Elvis Presley]]<ref>{{YouTube|rvGlDkQqxoc|Queen interview: Brian May on Crazy Little Thing Called Love}} Absolute Radio. Retrieved 18 December 2011</ref> and [[Cliff Richard]]. In a ''[[Melody Maker]]'' interview dated 2 May 1981, Mercury stated that he composed "Crazy Little Thing Called Love" on guitar in just five to ten minutes.<ref name=":1">{{cite web|url=http://www.queenarchives.com/index.php?title=Freddie_Mercury_-_05-02-1981_-_Melody_Maker|title=Queen Interviews – Freddie Mercury – 05-02-1981 – Melody Maker|date=2 May 1981|website=Queen Archives|publisher=[[Melody Maker]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101128105653/http://queenarchives.com/index.php?title=Freddie_Mercury_-_05-02-1981_-_Melody_Maker|archive-date=28 November 2010|url-status=dead|access-date=14 October 2016}}</ref>

{{quote|'Crazy Little Thing Called Love' took me five or ten minutes. I did that on the guitar, which I can't play for nuts, and in one way it was quite a good thing because I was restricted, knowing only a few chords. It's a good discipline because I simply had to write within a small framework. I couldn't work through too many chords and because of that restriction I wrote a good song, I think.|Freddie Mercury}}

According to [[Roger Taylor (Queen drummer)|Roger Taylor]], Mercury quickly completed the song's lyrics while relaxing in a bath at the [[Hotel Bayerischer Hof]] in [[Munich]] and presented them shortly afterward to him and [[John Deacon]].<ref name="Circus"/><ref name=":1" /><ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=TyQEAAAAMBAJ&dq=CRAZY+LITTLE+THING+CALLED+LOVE+-+MERCURY+-+Elvis+-+Billboard+-+12+July+1980&pg=PT32 Billboard 18 Jul 1980] p.33. Billboard. Retrieved 29 June 2011</ref> The three members, along with their then-new producer [[Reinhold Mack]], recorded it at [[Musicland Studios]], where Queen held sessions for their next album. The song was reportedly completed in under half an hour, although Mack later recalled that the session took six hours.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Interview with Reinhold Mack, Esq.|publisher=iZotope|url=http://www.izotope.com/artists/reinhold_mack.asp|access-date=24 April 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111014105317/http://izotope.com/artists/reinhold_mack.asp|archive-date=14 October 2011|url-status=dead}}</ref>

May's guitar solo was [[Overdubbing|dubbed]] in.<ref name=":0" /> He aimed to emulate longtime [[Ricky Nelson]] and Presley guitarist [[James Burton]], and, at Mack's suggestion, used a [[Fender Esquire]] rather than his regular [[Red Special]] to achieve this effect.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.musicradar.com/news/guitars/in-pictures-brian-mays-other-guitars-384279|title=Music Radar: Brian May's 'other' guitars|date=24 February 2011|website=[[MusicRadar]]|first=Simon|last=Bradley}}</ref>
sections.text:
The song was written by Mercury as a tribute to his musical heroes Elvis Presley and Cliff Richard. In a Melody Maker interview dated 2 May 1981, Mercury stated that he composed "Crazy Little Thing Called Love" on guitar in just five to ten minutes.

{{quote|'Crazy Little Thing Called Love' took me five or ten minutes. I did that on the guitar, which I can't play for nuts, and in one way it was quite a good thing because I was restricted, knowing only a few chords. It's a good discipline because I simply had to write within a small framework. I couldn't work through too many chords and because of that restriction I wrote a good song, I think.|Freddie Mercury}}

According to Roger Taylor, Mercury quickly completed the song's lyrics while relaxing in a bath at the Hotel Bayerischer Hof in Munich and presented them shortly afterward to him and John Deacon. The three members, along with their then-new producer Reinhold Mack, recorded it at Musicland Studios, where Queen held sessions for their next album. The song was reportedly completed in under half an hour, although Mack later recalled that the session took six hours.

May's guitar solo was dubbed in. He aimed to emulate longtime Ricky Nelson and Presley guitarist James Burton, and, at Mack's suggestion, used a Fender Esquire rather than his regular Red Special to achieve this effect.

sections.heading: Critical reception
sections.wikitext: "Crazy Little Thing Called Love" received acclaim from contemporary music critics. ''[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cashbox]]'' described it as a "hip shakin' rockabilly romp" and an "upbeat tune",<ref name="cb">{{cite news|title=Cash Box Singles Reviews|date=December 22, 1979|page=11|newspaper=[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cashbox]]|accessdate=2022-01-01|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Cash-Box/70s/1979/CB-1979-12-22.pdf}}</ref> while ''[[Record World]]'' said that the band "does a superb job of capturing the spirit and sound of the late '50s [[Bebop|be-bop]] rock'n'roll".<ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=[[Record World]]|date=December 22, 1979|accessdate=2023-02-11|title=Hits of the Week|page=1|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Record-World/70s/79/RW-1979-12-22.pdf}}</ref> ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' praised May's guitar playing, calling it "stunning in its simplicity".<ref>{{cite news|title=Top Singles Picks|magazine=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]|date=22 December 1979|page=76|access-date=7 July 2020|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-Billboard/70s/1979/Billboard%201979-12-22.pdf}}</ref>
sections.text: "Crazy Little Thing Called Love" received acclaim from contemporary music critics. Cashbox described it as a "hip shakin' rockabilly romp" and an "upbeat tune", while Record World said that the band "does a superb job of capturing the spirit and sound of the late '50s be-bop rock'n'roll". Billboard praised May's guitar playing, calling it "stunning in its simplicity".

sections.heading: Chart performance
sections.wikitext: In the United Kingdom, "Crazy Little Thing Called Love" entered the [[UK singles chart]] on 20 October 1979 and peaked at number two on 24 November, unable to dislodge "[[When You're in Love with a Beautiful Woman]]" by [[Dr. Hook]] from the top position for two weeks.<ref>{{Cite web |date=1979 |title=CRAZY LITTLE THING CALLED LOVE by QUEEN |url=https://www.officialcharts.com/songs/queen-crazy-little-thing-called-love/ |website=[[UK singles chart|Official Singles Chart]]}}</ref> In the United States, the song entered the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] on 22 December 1979 at number 58 before reaching number one on 23 February 1980, where it remained for four consecutive weeks, becoming Queen's first US number-one single.<ref name="UKSingles" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Database |first=Billboard |title=Crazy Little Thing Called Love / Queen |url=https://elpee.jp/single/Crazy%20Little%20Thing%20Called%20Love/Queen/ |access-date=2026-04-16 |website=elpee.jp |language=en}}</ref> The song also reached number one in Australia, Canada, and the Netherlands.<ref name="ARIA">[[David Kent (historian)|Kent, David]] (1993) (doc). [[Kent Music Report|Australian Chart Book 1970–1992]]. Australian Chart Book, St Ives, N.S.W</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=23 February 1980 |title=RPM 100 Singles |url=https://recherche-collection-search.bac-lac.gc.ca/eng/home/record?IdNumber=5984&app=rpm |access-date= |website=[[Library and Archives Canada]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=1979 |title=Queen – Crazy Little Thing Called Love |url=https://dutchcharts.nl/showitem.asp?interpret=Queen&titel=Crazy+Little+Thing+Called+Love&cat=s |language=nl}}</ref>
sections.text: In the United Kingdom, "Crazy Little Thing Called Love" entered the UK singles chart on 20 October 1979 and peaked at number two on 24 November, unable to dislodge "When You're in Love with a Beautiful Woman" by Dr. Hook from the top position for two weeks. In the United States, the song entered the Billboard Hot 100 on 22 December 1979 at number 58 before reaching number one on 23 February 1980, where it remained for four consecutive weeks, becoming Queen's first US number-one single. The song also reached number one in Australia, Canada, and the Netherlands.

sections.heading: Music video
sections.wikitext: The music video for the song, directed by Denis deVance, was filmed at Trillion Studios in [[London]] on 21 September 1979 and features four dancers, including Nikki Billyeald and Julie Warwick, as well as a floor made up of hands. An alternate version was later included on the ''Days of Our Lives'' DVD and Blu-ray releases.

sections.heading: Live performances
sections.wikitext:
Shortly after releasing the single, the band embarked on a mini tour across Ireland and the United Kingdom entitled the [[Crazy Tour]]. Having played acoustic rhythm guitar on the recording, Mercury played it in concert for the first time during the tour.<ref name="Circus" /><ref>[http://www.ultimatequeen.co.uk/songs/game.htm#crazy Crazy Little Thing Called Love] UltimateQueen. Retrieved 29 June 2011</ref>

In some live performances of the track, the band added an extended rock ending that brought the song to over five minutes, with May and Mercury playing guitar together. Piano parts were added in and typically performed by touring musician [[Spike Edney]].

The song was notably included on Queen's setlist for the 1985 [[Live Aid]] dual-venue [[benefit concert]].<ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0ORIoUohBUc |title=Queen - Crazy Little Thing Called Love (Live Aid 1985) |date= |last= |access-date= |via=[[YouTube]]}}</ref>
sections.text:
Shortly after releasing the single, the band embarked on a mini tour across Ireland and the United Kingdom entitled the Crazy Tour. Having played acoustic rhythm guitar on the recording, Mercury played it in concert for the first time during the tour.

In some live performances of the track, the band added an extended rock ending that brought the song to over five minutes, with May and Mercury playing guitar together. Piano parts were added in and typically performed by touring musician Spike Edney.

The song was notably included on Queen's setlist for the 1985 Live Aid dual-venue benefit concert.

sections.heading: Personnel
sections.wikitext:
*[[Freddie Mercury]] – lead and backing vocals, acoustic guitar, hand claps
*[[Brian May]] – backing vocals, electric guitar, hand claps
*[[Roger Taylor (Queen drummer)|Roger Taylor]] – backing vocals, drums, hand claps
*[[John Deacon]] – bass guitar, hand claps
Although Mercury played an acoustic-electric twelve-string [[Ovation Guitar Company|Ovation Pacemaker]] 1615 guitar and later an electric six-string [[Fender Telecaster]] (both owned by May) during live performances, he recorded the studio version of the song using a six-string acoustic guitar with external microphones. The original guitar recording has since been lost.<ref>{{cite magazine|title=May confirms Mercury played solo|magazine=Guitar & Bass|url=http://www.queencuttings.com/images/solo/Guitar%26Bass_jan2008_p05.jpg|access-date=24 September 2022|archive-date=16 December 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181216031235/http://www.queencuttings.com/images/solo/Guitar%26Bass_jan2008_p05.jpg|url-status=bot: unknown}}</ref>

American [[country music]] singer [[Dwight Yoakam]] included a cover of the song on his 1999 album ''[[Last Chance for a Thousand Years: Dwight Yoakam's Greatest Hits from the 90's]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url={{AllMusic|class=album|id=r420881|pure_url=yes}}|title=''Last Chance for a Thousand Years'' review|author=[[Stephen Thomas Erlewine]]|work=[[AllMusic]]|access-date=4 June 2009}}</ref> Yoakam's version was released as a single. It debuted at number 65 on the US ''Billboard'' "Hot Country Singles & Tracks" chart for the week of 1 May 1999, and peaked at number 12 on the US country singles charts that year. It was also used in a television commercial for clothing retailer [[Gap (clothing retailer)|Gap]] at the time of the album's release. The [[music video]] was directed by Yoakam. This version appears in the movie ''{{sortname|The|Break-Up}}'' (2006), starring [[Vince Vaughn]] and [[Jennifer Aniston]].

American country music singer Dwight Yoakam included a cover of the song on his 1999 album Last Chance for a Thousand Years: Dwight Yoakam's Greatest Hits from the 90's. Yoakam's version was released as a single. It debuted at number 65 on the US Billboard "Hot Country Singles & Tracks" chart for the week of 1 May 1999, and peaked at number 12 on the US country singles charts that year. It was also used in a television commercial for clothing retailer Gap at the time of the album's release. The music video was directed by Yoakam. This version appears in the movie {{sortname|The|Break-Up}} (2006), starring Vince Vaughn and Jennifer Aniston.
